## PWR Core Design

### Fuel Enrichment

Natural uranium is 0.72% U-235. PWR fuel is enriched to roughly 3–5% U-235, with modern reload batches often approaching the current regulatory limit of 5%. Higher enrichment supports longer fuel cycles (18–24 months is typical) and higher power density. Fresh assemblies at the core periphery are typically loaded at lower enrichment than interior assemblies to flatten the radial power distribution.

### Lattice Geometry and Rod Pitch

A standard PWR fuel pin is roughly 9.5 mm in diameter with a center-to-center pitch of about 12.6–13 mm, giving a P/D ratio around 1.33. The 17×17 assembly (Westinghouse AP1000 style) is the dominant modern configuration — 264 fuel rods, 24 guide tubes for control rods, one instrumentation tube.

The pitch sets the moderator-to-fuel volume ratio, which is the geometric handle on moderation level.

### Moderator Ratio and Why PWRs Are Undermoderated

The H/U atomic ratio in a typical PWR lattice sits around 3–4. Crucially, this places the lattice **to the left of the moderation peak** on a k-effective vs. H/U curve — meaning the reactor is deliberately undermoderated.

If you plot k-eff against hydrogen-to-uranium ratio, it peaks around H/U ≈ 5–6 and falls off on both sides. PWRs operate on the ascending (left) side. The practical consequence: increasing water density increases k, decreasing water density decreases k. That asymmetry is what makes the negative moderator temperature coefficient possible.

### Reactivity Coefficients

**Doppler coefficient (fuel temperature coefficient)**
The fastest feedback mechanism. As fuel temperature rises, the Doppler effect broadens the U-238 neutron capture resonances (especially around 6.7 eV). More neutrons are absorbed parasitically, fewer cause fissions. Response is essentially instantaneous because fuel temperature tracks power directly. Typically –1 to –3 pcm/°C. This is what prevents prompt power excursions from getting away before the moderator responds.

**Moderator temperature coefficient (MTC)**
As coolant temperature rises, water density drops. On an undermoderated lattice, lower density means less moderation, fewer thermal neutrons reaching fuel, reduced reactivity. The MTC must be maintained negative throughout the fuel cycle — typically in the range of –5 to –50 pcm/°C depending on boron concentration and burnup. At beginning-of-life with high dissolved boron (see below), the MTC is less negative; at end-of-life with low boron, it's more negative. Tech specs set a negative MTC limit.

**Void coefficient**
If bulk boiling occurs and steam voids form, moderation drops sharply. The void coefficient is strongly negative in PWRs — opposite to the RBMK, where the positive void coefficient contributed to Chernobyl. High operating pressure (~155 bar) keeps bulk boiling suppressed under normal operation, so this coefficient is a defense-in-depth feature rather than a routine control mechanism.

**Power coefficient**
The net reactivity change per unit power change, combining Doppler and moderator effects. Must be negative at all power levels. Typically –10 to –20 pcm/% power. It's the operationally relevant metric because it describes self-correction during load transients.

### The Self-Stabilization Picture

The two coefficients work on different timescales. Doppler responds in milliseconds as fuel temperature tracks neutron flux. If a positive reactivity insertion occurs, Doppler immediately adds negative reactivity to partially offset it, limiting how fast power can rise before the moderator (which heats on a timescale of seconds) adds its own negative feedback. Together they create an inherently stable system: a step power increase drives both mechanisms negative, reducing reactivity until a new equilibrium is reached at a slightly higher temperature.

### Dissolved Boron

Boric acid dissolved in the primary coolant (typically 1000–2000 ppm at beginning of cycle, decreasing to near zero at end of cycle) handles long-term reactivity management as fuel burns up. Its concentration coefficient is negative, but it's adjusted slowly via the CVCS rather than providing dynamic feedback. The boron concentration also affects MTC — higher boron shifts the neutron spectrum and reduces the negative MTC — which is why MTC limits are verified against boron concentration and burnup state in the tech specs.
